back: A feedback control system whose signals are measured, processed and generated at discrete instants: ADC → digital controller → DAC → plant.
Sampling (discretise time), quantisation (discretise amplitude), encoding (binary code).

front: Advantages and disadvantages of digital control
back: Advantages: lower cost, flexibility (reprogrammable). Disadvantages: limited by the sampling frequency, needs an ADC and a DAC, computational delay.
Measuring a continuous signal at uniform intervals: $x(k) = x(kT_s)$.
Under-sampled high frequencies appear as false lower frequencies, $|f - nf_s|$. Prevent it with $f_s \ge 2f_{max}$ and an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC.
A band-limited signal can be reconstructed if $f_s \ge 2f_{max}$. $2f_{max}$ is the Nyquist rate; $f_s/2$ is the Nyquist frequency.
In practice $f_s$ = 5–10 × $f_{max}$, and at least 10 × the closed-loop bandwidth for control.
$\Delta = (V_{max} - V_{min})/2^n$; maximum error $\pm\Delta/2$; resolution $1/2^n \times 100\%$.
$X(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty x(k)z^{-k}$; $z^{-1}$ is a one-sample delay; $z = e^{sT}$.
The set of $z$ for which the series converges. Causal: outside the outermost pole. Stable: includes the unit circle.
$a^k \leftrightarrow \dfrac{z}{z - a}$, $|z| > |a|$. Step: $z/(z - 1)$. Impulse: 1.
$kT \leftrightarrow Tz/(z - 1)^2$; $e^{-akT} \leftrightarrow z/(z - e^{-aT})$.
Right: $\mathcal{Z}\{x(k - n)\} = z^{-n}X(z)$. Left: $\mathcal{Z}\{x(k + 1)\} = zX(z) - zx(0)$.
$x(0) = \lim_{z\to\infty}X(z)$; $x(\infty) = \lim_{z\to1}(z - 1)X(z)$ (if the final value exists).
$G(z) = Y(z)/U(z) = \dfrac{b_0 + b_1z^{-1} + \cdots}{1 + a_1z^{-1} + \cdots}$. Poles give stability; zeros shape the response.
Power series (long division), partial fractions (on $X(z)/z$), residues ($\frac{1}{2\pi j}\oint X(z)z^{k - 1}dz$).
The inverse z-transform gives values only at $t = kT$; $z/(z - 1)$ is any function equal to 1 at the sampling instants.
Holds each sample constant for one period (a staircase); $G_{h0}(s) = (1 - e^{-sT})/s$; a low-pass filter with an average delay of $T/2$.
$G(z) = (1 - z^{-1})\mathcal{Z}\{G(s)/s\}$: divide by $s$, transform, multiply by $(z - 1)/z$.
$\dfrac1a\cdot\dfrac{1 - e^{-aT}}{z - e^{-aT}}$ (the slides omit the $1/a$).
$s = \dfrac2T\cdot\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1}$; preserves stability, no aliasing, but frequency warping (pre-warp critical frequencies).
Blocks in one continuous path (no sampler between) are multiplied in $s$ first: $G_1G_2(z) \ne G_1(z)G_2(z)$.

front: Loop with a forward sampler only
back: $T(z) = \dfrac{G(z)}{1 + GH(z)}$. With samplers in both paths: $\dfrac{G(z)}{1 + G(z)H(z)}$.
They can be added at the output of a block with a sampled input, or at the inputs of a summing junction whose output is sampled (if synchronised).
All poles $|z| < 1$: stable. Any $|z| > 1$: unstable. Simple poles on $|z| = 1$: marginal. Repeated on $|z| = 1$: unstable.
A pole at $z = a$ gives a mode $a^k$, which decays only if $|a| < 1$. $z = e^{sT}$ maps the left half-plane inside the circle.
Bounded input gives bounded output ⇔ $\sum|h(k)| < \infty$ ⇔ all poles inside the unit circle.
Substitute $z = (s + 1)/(s - 1)$, clear the denominators, apply Routh–Hurwitz: if $D(s)$ is stable, so is $D(z)$.
A large $T$ can make a stable analog loop unstable: for $K/[s(s + 1)]$ with a ZOH, the largest $K$ is 20.3 at $T = 0.1$ s and 1.46 at $T = 2$ s.
Stability, accuracy (small steady-state error), speed (fast rise), robustness.
$K\dfrac{z - z_0}{z - p_0}$ with $0 < z_0 < p_0 < 1$ (pole nearer $z = 1$): raises the DC gain, so a smaller steady-state error but a slower response.
$K\dfrac{z - z_0}{z - p_0}$ with $0 < p_0 < z_0 < 1$ (zero nearer $z = 1$): adds phase, giving a faster rise, less overshoot and more phase margin.
$C(z) = K_p + \dfrac{K_iTz}{z - 1} + \dfrac{K_d}{T}\cdot\dfrac{z - 1}{z}$; the integrator pole at $z = 1$ removes the step error.
The closed-loop poles as $K$ varies, with the usual rules; stability boundary = the unit circle. $K(z + 0.5)/[z(z - 0.8)]$ is stable for $0 < K < 2$.
$u[k] = -Kx[k]$ gives $x[k + 1] = (A - BK)x[k]$; place the eigenvalues of $A - BK$ inside the unit circle.
$\beta\dfrac{1 + \tau s}{1 + \beta\tau s}$, $\tau = R_1C$, $\beta = R_2/(R_1 + R_2) < 1$: the zero is nearer the origin.
$\dfrac{1 + \tau s}{1 + \beta\tau s}$, $\tau = R_2C$, $\beta = (R_1 + R_2)/R_2 > 1$: the pole is nearer the origin.
The angle a lead compensator must add at $s_d$ so that the total angle is ±180°: $\phi = 180° - \angle G(s_d)$.
$H(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D$; the poles are the eigenvalues of $A$.
